blocks.instruction: Leia o texto e escolha a alternativa correta. Algumas perguntas pedem inferência — a resposta não está escrita com todas as letras.
blocks.passage:
Designing a logistics network, at this level, starts from the customer map — not from the current warehouse list. The first question is simple: where are our customers, and how quickly do they expect their orders? From there, you work backward to decide where warehouses, hubs and routes should sit.

A good network usually has a small number of hubs placed to shorten the longest trips, not the shortest ones. Moving a warehouse 20 km closer to a small customer barely changes anything. Moving it closer to the biggest cluster of customers often rewrites the whole cost and service picture.

If you were designing this network from scratch today, you would almost always choose a different shape from the one you inherited. The real question is not whether a better design exists — it usually does — but whether the change is worth the disruption.

items.q: According to the text, where should a network design start?
options: From the location of the head office
items.why: "Designing a logistics network… starts from the customer map — not from the current warehouse list."

items.q: Where should the small number of hubs be placed?
options: As close to head office as possible
items.why: "a small number of hubs placed to shorten the longest trips, not the shortest ones."

items.q: Why does moving a warehouse closer to the biggest cluster matter more?
options: Because it is always cheaper to build there
Because it reduces the number of hubs to one
Because small customers order more often
Because it often rewrites the whole cost and service picture
items.why: "Moving it closer to the biggest cluster of customers often rewrites the whole cost and service picture."

items.q: The author would most likely DISAGREE with which statement?
options: Customer location should drive the network shape.
The longest trips deserve the most attention.
A better design often exists but may not be worth the disruption.
An inherited network is usually the best possible one.
items.why: Inferência: o texto diz que, do zero, você quase sempre escolheria uma forma diferente da herdada — logo, a rede herdada raramente é a melhor.

items.q: What does the last paragraph SUGGEST about redesigning a network?
options: Knowing a better design exists is not enough to justify changing
A better design almost never exists in practice
The inherited shape is impossible to improve
items.why: Inferência: existe quase sempre um design melhor, mas a decisão depende de o ganho compensar a disrupção.

blocks.instruction: Ouça Harry conduzindo a revisão da rede com um novo analista. Responda sem ler a transcrição — ela só aparece depois de corrigir.

audio.text:
Okay, come and look at the map with me. Forget the warehouse list for a minute — I want you to see where the customers actually are. See this cluster here, in the south? That's where most of our volume sits now. It wasn't like that five years ago.

Our main hub is up here, in the old industrial park. If we moved it about forty kilometres south, closer to that cluster, we would cut the longest delivery trips by nearly a day. That's the number that matters. Shaving ten minutes off a short local run does almost nothing.

Now, here's the interesting part. Everyone assumed the answer was to close the second site to save money. But if you close that site, you lose the coverage in the north entirely. Move the main hub instead, and you'd save more than closing a whole warehouse — and you'd keep the coverage.

So before you touch a spreadsheet, ask one thing: if we were building this from scratch today, would we ever put the hub where it is now? Almost certainly not. Then the only real question is whether the saving is worth the disruption of moving it.
audio.label: Ouça quantas vezes precisar. A transcrição aparece depois de corrigir.

items.q: What does Harry ask the analyst to look at FIRST?
options: The cost of the second site
items.why: "Forget the warehouse list for a minute — I want you to see where the customers actually are."

items.q: What would happen if the main hub moved 40 km south?
options: It would close the second site automatically
It would save ten minutes on short local runs
It would cut the longest delivery trips by nearly a day
It would move all customers to the south
items.why: "we would cut the longest delivery trips by nearly a day."

items.q: According to Harry, what is the problem with closing the second site?
options: It would lose the coverage in the north entirely
It has the biggest cluster of customers
It costs too much to close
items.why: "if you close that site, you lose the coverage in the north entirely."

items.q: Why does Harry mention that the cluster 'wasn't like that five years ago'?
options: To say the data is unreliable
To suggest the network no longer matches where customers are today
To explain why the second site was built
To argue the hub should never move
items.why: Inferência: os clientes migraram, então a rede herdada ficou desalinhada com a realidade atual.

items.q: What does Harry imply by asking 'would we ever put the hub where it is now?'
options: The location was chosen deliberately for today's map
The hub should be closed instead of moved
The current location is clearly the best choice
From scratch, nobody would choose the current spot
items.why: Inferência: a pergunta retórica sugere que, do zero, ninguém escolheria o local atual — ele foi herdado.

blocks.instruction: O vocabulário da lição aparece aqui em frases novas. Escolha o sentido ou a palavra que cabe no contexto.

items.q: "We plotted every order on a customer map before touching the routes." A customer map is…
options: the delivery schedule for one week
a diagram of the reporting lines
a picture of where the customers and their demand are
items.why: Customer map = mapa de clientes: onde eles estão e quanto pedem.

items.q: "Instead of starting from the sites, we worked backward from the customers." To work backward means to…
options: count the trips in reverse order
start from the goal and reason toward the steps
items.why: To work backward = trabalhar de trás para frente: partir do resultado e voltar até as decisões.

items.q: Choose the correct word: "Most of our volume sits in one dense ___ of customers in the south."
items.why: Cluster = aglomerado: um grupo denso de clientes numa região.

items.q: "If we redesigned it from scratch, the network would look completely different." From scratch means…
options: from the beginning, with nothing inherited
using the current sites as a base
items.why: From scratch = do zero, sem partir de nada existente.

items.q: "We inherited this hub location from a decision made a decade ago." To inherit here means to…
options: receive and keep something set up by others earlier
items.why: To inherit = herdar: receber algo já montado por decisões anteriores.

blocks.instruction: Expressões que aparecem em revisões de rede logística. Escolha o sentido no contexto.

items.q: "Moving the hub 40 km south would really move the needle on delivery times." This means it would…
items.why: Move the needle = mexer o ponteiro, fazer diferença perceptível.

items.q: "The operations director still has to sign off on the new network." To sign off on means to…
items.why: Sign off on = aprovar formalmente, dar o aval final.

items.q: "We'll roll out the new routes region by region." To roll out means to…
items.why: Roll out = implementar de forma progressiva.

items.q: "Two regional managers pushed back on closing the northern site." They…
items.why: Push back on = resistir, discordar — sem necessariamente rejeitar de vez.

items.q: "The savings look good, but they don't outweigh the disruption of moving." To outweigh means to…
options: be more important than something else
items.why: Outweigh = pesar mais, superar em importância — aqui, o ganho não supera a disrupção.
